sentences: The police raid a premises at night and find a priest at an open safe: he explains he is replacing the money for a parishioner.
He is arrested and put in the cells but released when the Monsignor confirms he is the priest.
Outside, the priest meets his erring parishioner the driver (an actor) and convinces him to be a chauffeur to his friend the noblewoman, rather than drive get-away cars.
The priest is chosen to go to the holy city carrying a 1,200-year-old priceless crucifix.
He is aware that his rival, the arch-criminal the thief, may try to steal the cross.
He sails to the foreign country and then catches a train.
The first stop is the capital, where he is accompanied by a priest he met on the ship.
As they sit in a cafe they are aware that two policemen are watching.
They wait until there are only two seats left on an excursion bus then grab it, leaving the police stranded.
The two police get a lift in the back of a police van with a group of prostitutes.
The excursion goes to the catacombs.
There the two priests separate from the group.
The priest has worked out that the other priest is really the thief, as he ordered a ham sandwich (on a Friday).
Nevertheless, the thief overpowers him and steals the cross, leaving the priest tied against a pile of bones.
The thief changes disguise and gets past the two police who wait at the entrance.
The priest convinces the noblewoman to auction an important silver chess set to lure the thief into stealing it.
They expect him to appear in disguise at the auction.
He does, but not as a bidder: the thief is the porter who carries the set out of the room after the bidding concludes.
But the thief returns the set to the noblewoman to prove a point.
When the police arrive at the door the thief and the priest remove all the milk from the back of a milk van to make it look as if they needed the space.
This diversion makes the police follow the van and the priest and the thief escape.
The priest starts researching the thief in the library, breaking his glasses in this task.
He finds a link to the town of the small town in the wine region of the foreign country.
He then goes there, and finds the thief at a wine festival, but the thief slips away.
The next day the priest finds the old chateau and asks for "the duke," but is told he is not home.
He slips into the inner courtyard disguised as an old woman on a cart of grapes.
On entering the chateau he finds signs of habitation, but the chateau is decrepit.
He discovers a secret door in the back of the big kitchen fireplace, and the thief asks him to enter.
Inside he has a priceless art collection.
He gives the priest the stolen cross.
The police arrive and the thief flees through the window.
His art collection is retrieved by the police and displayed in the museum.
Back in his home country, the priest gives a sermon on the parable.
The thief enters and sits next to the noblewoman.
Showman the carnival man (who works contracting sleazy acts for a freakshow carnival) is contacted by an old friend the blackmailed man who has received a blackmail letter signed "a woman's name".
The carnival man agrees to check her out as she lives near a friend of his.
Reaching her apartment, he discovers she is an old pal of his named the blackmailer, who has fallen on hard times and got mixed up with someone she regrets.
She agrees to withdraw her blackmail attempt, as it was not her idea.
In the apartment downstairs the carnival man offers to set up his Russian friend, the performer, in a freakshow "starvation act" in a glass cage to break the world record.
A party is hastily arranged for that night for their carnival pals.
In the evening, the performer sees a man going up to the blackmailer's room.
During the party the blackmailer is found murdered.
The chief suspect is the blackmailed man because his blackmail letter was discovered near her body.

Unsavoury character the crook first attempts to blackmail another suspect, who he knows had a motive; and then also the blackmailed man, but the latter draws a gun and in a struggle it is the blackmailed man who is killed.
The crook tries to frighten the carnival man by kidnapping his wife, but she escapes and the police arrest the crook.
The carnival man tries to get the performer to remember who he saw on the night of the blackmailer's murder while he was "starving" in a glass cage.
Someone passes strychnine-laced food inside the cage and the performer, suffering from the poisoning, breaks the glass and accidentally kills himself.
His death is covered up by the carnival man and the police to tempt the poisoner to come back to finish the job.
He falls for the trick and returns only to be confronted by police and shot dead while trying to escape.
While playing tennis at a posh club in a town near the capital called the suburb, young and flirty the tennis player attracts considerable interest.
The men ogle her and the women detest her.
She is later found dead, strangled with a stocking.
The local police chief requests the help of the national police headquarters, so the detective is sent to investigate.
The locals, however, resent having an outsider poking into their affairs.
A book of love poems, including an inscription from a young man, is found in the victim's flat.
There is also a photo of a group of men together with the tennis player and the heiress, a young woman from the prominent local family.
Her father the patriarch, although shocked to learn that his daughter knew the "trashy" tennis player, will not let the detective question her.
The detective eventually learns that the tennis player left the young man for a married man, the club official, who is the club's secretary.
The club official denies any involvement, and also claims that he was giving nurse the young nurse a lift to her hospital at the time of the murder.
The coroner the pathologist reveals the tennis player was two months pregnant.
The doctor, the local Canadian expat physician who certified the death, is asked by the detective why he neglected to report that fact.
The doctor claims he was trying to avoid a scandal for the club official and the club.
The young nurse turns out to be the doctor's niece and also a Canadian expat.
She confirms that the club official gave her a lift, but this later turns out to be a lie.
A result of her attempts to protect the reputation of her uncle, who left his practice in his home city after a misdiagnosis led to a patient's death.
This is something the locals are unaware of, but the club official knows and is using this secret to blackmail the doctor.

The club official, always bragging about his wartime heroics as an air force fighter pilot who achieved the rank of Wing Commander, is revealed by the detective to have been nothing but a lowly ground crew member, who was dishonourably discharged after theft and is currently heavily in debt.
The club demands the club official's resignation.
He turns up at a party, gets drunk and starts a fight.
Leaving the party and going for a walk, the heiress is ambushed and strangled to death.
Her body is placed in the boot of the doctor's car.
The detective finds out that the young man has been treated for schizophrenia.
The young man flees to a church, climbs to the top of the steeple and threatens to jump.
The detective ascends the steeple to prevent the suicide, risking his own life in the process, and manages to convince the young man not to kill himself.
A fire brigade turntable ladder rescues the two just as they are about to fall.
While travelling by train, the amateur sleuth witnesses the strangling of a young woman in another train on a parallel track.

The police find nothing to support her story, so she conducts her own investigation, and with the aid of her close friend the helper, comes to the conclusion that the body must have been thrown off the train near the grounds of the manor house.
Wheedling her way into a job as housekeeper, the amateur sleuth copes with her difficult employer, the old landowner, and searches for the missing corpse.
She eventually finds it concealed in a stable, much to the chagrin of the police inspector.

The helper uncovers the details of the old landowner's will: the family fortune is to go to his long-suffering, attentive daughter the heiress; his sons the first son, the second son and the third son; and the boy, his intelligent and insightful grandson (A fourth son, the soldier, was killed in the war and a second daughter, the late daughter, the boy's mother, died of illness).
Also, the doctor, the old landowner's physician, and the heiress are secretly in love.
The gardener, the groundsman, and the part-time servant the cleaning woman round out the establishment and the list of suspects.
The boy finds the first clue, a musical compact that plays "a French nursery song", near where the body must have landed.

When the heiress reveals that she recently received a letter from a French woman named the claimant, who claims that she married the soldier shortly before he died and is therefore an heir, the identity of the dead woman and the motive for the crime seem clear.
Arsenic in the curried duck prepared by the amateur sleuth sickens all who eat it, but only the third son dies.
Then the second son is killed by his own shotgun.
The police are unsure if it was suicide by a remorseful murderer or the third victim.
The amateur sleuth, however, is not deceived, and sets a trap, using the compact as bait.
The doctor is revealed as the villain.
The dead woman was not the claimant at all, but his own wife.
The doctor feared that the compact, a gift to his wife, could be traced to him.
He intended to dispose of the other heirs and marry the heiress.
He administered a second, fatal dose of arsenic while supposedly attending to the third son.
As with most of her portrayals of the amateur sleuth, the leading actress's interpretation was quite different from the author's.
In addition, the author's suspense and underlying darkness are largely replaced by light, even whimsical touches typical of a comedy of manners.
In the novel, an elderly woman named the traveller witnesses the murder, not her friend, the amateur sleuth, who is introduced later.
Also in the novel, a young acquaintance of the amateur sleuth's, not the amateur sleuth herself, is sent to pose as a housekeeper at the suspect location.

The manor house where the amateur sleuth conducts her enquiries is called the original manor name in the novel, but this was changed to the manor house in the film to avoid using the leading actress's surname.
The original surname, the family name in the novel, was shortened to the film surname.
While the amateur sleuth and the helper are soliciting donations for a charity ("a charity for reformed criminals"), they call on the old man, a rich recluse.
He tumbles down the long entrance staircase, apparently the victim of a fatal heart attack.
Knowing that the old man had a pathological fear of cats, the amateur sleuth becomes suspicious when she finds one in the house.
She also finds a piece of mud bearing the print of a riding boot, but when she goes to the police inspector, he is sceptical, believing that the old man died of natural causes.
Undeterred, the amateur sleuth eavesdrops when the old man's family gather for the reading of the will.
There are four beneficiaries: fourth cousin the horseman, niece the young wife, nephew the hotelier and sister the old man's sister.
Each receives an equal share of the estate.
The old man's sister claims that the old man was murdered.
The next day, when the amateur sleuth goes to see her, she finds the old man's sister dead, stabbed in the back with a hatpin.
The old man's sister's companion of many years, timid the mousy woman, can provide little information.
The amateur sleuth begins her investigations as a guest at the hotel run by the hotelier, where the other two surviving heirs and the mousy woman are staying.
When the police inspector questions them and the young wife's spendthrift husband the spouse, none of them can produce a satisfactory alibi for the time of the old man's sister's death.
An attempt is made to do away with the amateur sleuth but is foiled by the intended victim (without her even realising it).

The amateur sleuth then discovers that the piece of mud found in the old man's house came from shady art dealer the horseman's riding boot, but her case against him is dashed when she learns that each of the heirs visited the old man on the day he died, to ask for money.
The horseman has meanwhile found out who the murderer is, but he is locked in a stall with an excitable horse and is trampled to death.
By this point, the amateur sleuth suspects the identity and motive of the killer but has no definite proof.
She, therefore, lays a trap, pretending to have a heart attack at a dance at the hotel while doing the twist with the helper.
The police doctor places her in a room by herself, declaring it to be too dangerous to move her until morning.
During the night, the murderer, the mousy woman impersonating the old man's sister, makes one last attempt to silence her, but the amateur sleuth is ready.
The mousy woman's motive is revealed to be a seemingly worthless painting owned by the old man's sister, which actually was very valuable.
The hotelier later proposes marriage to the amateur sleuth but she turns him down.
When she declares her distaste for blood sports, the hotelier, an enthusiastic fox hunter, mutters to himself "That was a narrow escape!"
An old wooden-walled warship, the training ship, has been purchased by a trust for the rehabilitation of young criminals.

Shortly after joining the board of the trust, the amateur sleuth witnesses the sudden death of a fellow trustee, who has just returned from a surprise visit to the ship, much disturbed by something he saw there.
He dies without revealing his discovery.
The amateur sleuth obtains a sample of his snuff, which is found to have been poisoned.
Resolving to learn what the trustee discovered, she visits the ship, while her confidant the helper investigates on shore.
The captain takes an immediate dislike to her, and makes a sarcastic comment to the first mate.
His distress intensifies when she decides to remain on board several days, and to sleep in the captain's quarters, obliging him to move into the first mate's cabin.
That night the amateur sleuth signals to the helper to request that he tail the sailors who just went ashore.
The helper finds that they are robbing houses, and takes their dinghy to row to the ship and inform the amateur sleuth.
The lieutenant overhears their conversation and is heading down to tell the Captain when he is murdered with a sword and then hanged from a mast.
As the police investigation proceeds, the assistant matron is killed, apparently by an injection of poison.
The investigation interferes with the ship's traditional celebration of Trafalgar Day.
The captain blames the amateur sleuth, and begs the chief inspector to find a way to get her off the ship.
The amateur sleuth sets a trap.
First, she persuades the chief inspector to allow the crew to go ashore for their Trafalgar Day celebration.
Then, she announces to the crew that she knows that the poison was administered using a mousetrap as a booby-trap, and she hints that she soon will reveal the murderer's identity.
With the crew ashore, the chief inspector and his assistant the sergeant hide in the ship to watch for the murderer.
As the amateur sleuth snoops around, she encounters the lieutenant commander skulking about.
He says he stayed behind due to seasickness.
The amateur sleuth searches the ship for the loaded mousetrap, cautiously using a sword to poke into possible hiding places.
She finds the mousetrap concealed in the barrel of a cannon, and with it, a large sum of money.
The first mate, armed with his sword, confronts her.

In response to her questioning, he informs her that he has embezzled the money gradually during his many years on the training ship – money he considers his because he was unjustly passed over for promotion while serving in the navy.
He acknowledges having committed the three preceding murders to avoid being exposed, and adds that he intends to kill her on the spot, take the money, and flee the country.
The amateur sleuth calls out to the chief inspector to make the arrest, but the chief inspector and the sergeant have been accidentally locked in their hiding place and cannot help.
The first mate draws his sword, intending to run the amateur sleuth through, but the amateur sleuth is herself an accomplished amateur fencer.
She and the first mate engage in a ferocious sword-fight.
The first mate succeeds in disarming her and is about to administer the coup de grace, but the helper, whom the amateur sleuth had thought was ashore, clubs him with a belaying pin.
The Captain faces a court martial for failing to detect the embezzlement under his command.
As he enters the state-room to hear the verdict, he sees his sword on the table with the hilt toward him, and mistakenly infers that he has been found guilty.
The amateur sleuth corrects him; the board has found that he is not at fault.
Although greatly relieved to have avoided disgrace, he announces that he must resign even so, because he has been having a long affair with the ship's matron.
They now intend to get married, which would disqualify him for his position as Captain.
He turns to go, but the trustees allow him to continue as captain.
He and the matron embrace joyfully.
As the amateur sleuth leaves the, the matron and the captain wave good-bye.
The lead actor begins the movie by talking directly to the audience.
He explains that he will be starring as the Belgian detective the sleuth in a mystery set in the capital.
As the movie begins, the sleuth has arrived in the capital to see his tailor.
There, he learns that a circus clown with a unique diving act has been murdered (with a poison dart), and the sleuth decides to solve the case.
He is joined in this endeavor by the agent from the British intelligence service, who has been assigned to protect the sleuth, or at least follow him.
The agent becomes the sleuth's assistant, of a sort.
Soon afterwards, a voluptuous bowling instructor is killed.

The clown was named the first victim (the first letter doubled), the bowling instructor was named the second victim (the second letter doubled) and both crime scenes featured a "calling card" from the killer: a book entitled "the alphabetical guide."
Of course, the sleuth suspects the killer is working his or her way through the alphabet.
While getting a massage, the sleuth is attacked by a beautiful woman.
We are left to conclude that the attack was intended to prevent the famous sleuth from solving the crimes.
We learn that she carried a purse with the initials of the first three letters.
Later we discover that her full name is the troubled woman.
The sleuth suggests that the knight (the third letter doubled) might be next.
We also meet a psychiatrist named the analyst (the fourth letter doubled) who is established as a potential fourth victim.
The troubled woman is actually a patient of the analyst's.
And secretly, the analyst was paramour to the second victim, and he is also having an affair with the knight's wife, the lady.
The sleuth learns that the troubled woman suffers from a split personality--one of her identities is that of a normal person, while the other seems to be a homicidal maniac.
Indeed, she is the beautiful woman who attacked the sleuth on the massage table.
The knight goes to a night club, to confront his brother the gambler over the gambler's spendthrift and gambling behaviors.
During the confrontation, the knight is shot and killed.
Again with a poison dart, and again with a copy of the alphabetical guide left behind.
The analyst is next--also with the poison dart, also with a copy of the alphabetical guide.
This makes four murders.
As the police and the sleuth focus their attention on the troubled woman, she apparently learns what she has done and jumps from a tall crane into the river.

The police close their investigation, calling it "open and shut" that the troubled woman was a "nutcase" intent on this bizarre series of alphabetical murders, eventually committing suicide to wrap things up.
The sleuth is not at all convinced.
Indeed a happenstance mention of herring inspires the sleuth to exclaim, "Red herrings.
The four murders are red herrings to distract us from the important one murder."
The gambler and the newly-widowed lady set off by train to carry out the knight's wishes to be buried at sea off the coast of the northern country.
The knight's coffin is on the train.

When the sleuth and the agent go to the knight's house in the capital, it is there that they learn what the gambler and the lady are doing--and in a moment of foreshadowing, they also learn that the house's central heating furnace has curiously been turned up, even though it is quite warm outside.
Immediately, the sleuth and the agent book passage on the train.
The sleuth makes an inscrutable detour en-route to the station, to set up "some additional insurance."
In their cabin, while the lady celebrates her new-found riches with the gambler, she fails to notice that he has spiked her drink.
She passes out, and he drags her to the storage compartment on the train where the knight's coffin is located.
At the coffin, two things happen: the sleuth arrives to confront the gambler, and the coffin is opened, from within, to reveal a not-dead-at-all troubled woman.
The sleuth unravels the mystery: the troubled woman and the gambler are lovers.
They conspire to kill the knight and the lady, so that the gambler can inherit the knight's fortune.
The troubled woman does the dart gun killings in a manner to fool the police.
American single mother the young woman, who recently moved to the capital from her home city, arrives at the preschool to collect her daughter, the little girl.
The child has mysteriously disappeared.
An administrator recalls meeting the young woman but claims never to have seen the missing child.

Pressed to be back home in time for an appointment with the movers, the young woman had been unable to wait to hand the little girl over in person to the administrator; she had been instructed by another employee to leave the little girl in a waiting room with another child and parent.
The young woman and her brother the young man search the school and find a peculiar old woman living upstairs, who claims she collects children's nightmares.
In desperation, the family call the police, and the superintendent arrives on the scene.
Everyone becomes a suspect, and the superintendent is steadfast, diligently following every lead.
The superintendent and the police decide to visit the family's new residence.
All of the little girl's possessions have been removed from the family's new home.
The young woman cannot understand why anyone would do this and reacts emotionally.

The superintendent begins to suspect that the little girl does not exist, particularly after the young man informs him that "the little girl's name" was the name of the young woman's imaginary childhood friend.

Hoping to verify the little girl's existence on the manifest, the superintendent asks the young man for the name of the ship on which the young woman and the little girl were passengers on the trip to the new country.
The young man argues with the superintendent, angrily asserting that he will hire a private detective to find the little girl, and storms off.
Deciding to become better acquainted with the young woman to learn more about the little girl, the superintendent takes the young woman to a local pub where he plies her with brandy and soda.
On her return home, the young woman discovers she still has the claim ticket for the little girl's doll, which she had taken to a doll hospital for repairs.
Regarding the doll as proof of the little girl's existence, she frantically rushes to the doll hospital late at night and retrieves the doll.

When the young woman shows the young man the doll, affirming that the doll’s existence proves the little girl’s existence, the young man takes the doll and sets it on fire, hoping to destroy it, then knocks the young woman unconscious.
The young man takes the unconscious young woman to a hospital, informing the desk nurse that the young woman has been hallucinating about a missing girl who does not exist.
The young woman is put under observation with instructions for her to be sedated if she awakes.
The young woman wakes up in the hospital and escapes.

Discovering the young man burying the little girl's possessions in the garden, the young woman then finds a bound and gagged little girl, who the young man had taken from the preschool, sedated, and hidden in the trunk of his car.

The young man reveals an incestuous interest with his sister, complaining that the little girl has always come between them, starting with when the young woman became pregnant from a relationship with her boyfriend.
Resenting that the young woman loves the little girl more than him, the young man wishes to eliminate the little girl, who threatens his dream of a future with his sister.
Realizing her brother is insane, the young woman begins playing childhood games with the young man, hoping to distract him from killing the little girl and to facilitate their escape.
Reverting back to childhood interaction, the young woman demands that they play Hide and Seek, with the young man being blindfolded while the young woman and the little girl "hide."
While the young man is blindfolded and counting, the young woman and the little girl run to escape, but soon the young man is done counting and begins the chase.

Unable to outrun the young man, the young woman and the little girl attempt to hide, with the young woman locking the little girl in a greenhouse and attempting to misdirect the young man away from her.
The young woman's attempt to secure the little girl fails when she discovers that the young man had hidden in the greenhouse and has captured the little girl.

Desperate to distract the young man, and playing for time, the young woman insists that she's bored with hide and seek and demands that the young man push her higher and higher on the nearby swing set.
Enthralled by his sister's attention, the young man temporarily loses focus on the little girl.
Having discovered that the young man lied to the police about the name of the ship that brought the family to the new country, the superintendent rushes quickly to the family's residence.
He arrives in time to apprehend the young man, successfully rescuing the young woman and the little girl.
Ten people travel by aerial tramway to a snowbound mansion, invited there by a stranger.
The stranger (Unknown) to spend the weekend.
They discover that none of them has actually ever met the stranger, including his secretary as well as a married housekeeper and cook, all hired through an agency.
Framed copies of the children's nursery rhyme about ten little Indians are hung on the walls of each guest's bedroom.
Dinner is served by the butler on a tray adorned with ten little Indian figurines, as well.
At exactly 9 p.m., as instructed, the butler switches on a hidden tape recording.
A man identifying himself as the stranger reveals that each of the 10 guests has a scandalous secret, their involvement in various innocent people's deaths.
One by one, the guests begin dying off.
One of the guests chokes after taking a drink and dies, and a small Indian figurine from the centrepiece tray is broken away.
In the morning, the tram cable is cut, killing the cook, the butler's wife, who attempted to escape.
The general conducts a search of the chalet's catacombs, splitting everyone into pairs, ultimately leading to his demise, stabbed after being led to a planted distraction (a cat).
It becomes clear that their unseen killer is following the nursery rhyme.

The young woman, the secretary, enters into a romantic relationship with the engineer as they and the others begin a deadly cat-and-mouse game, ultimately deducing that the stranger is not their host but, in reality, one of them.
After falling under suspicion from the others, the butler attempts to make his escape down the mountain peak, the cliff, ending in his death after his lifeline is severed with an axe.
Another guest bitterly confesses to having driven her husband to suicide, and is later found dead in her bedroom, killed with a syringe.
By now, the five remaining guests fall under distrust of one another, and alliances are formed as the generator shuts down, casting the mansion into total darkness.

At dinner, each person reveals the nature of their accusations, but before the young woman can attest to her crime, she separates from the group to her room, where she screams upon discovering an Indian decoy hung from the ceiling.
In the confusion, the judge is found with a gunshot wound to his head.
The doctor intimates his suspicions of the young woman, which the engineer angrily rebuffs.
The engineer later comes to the young woman's room and confides that his real name is another name, and that the real engineer, a friend of the impostor's, had committed suicide.
Sorting out the real engineer's things, the impostor found the invitation and decided to accept it, posing as the real engineer, to see if he could throw light on why his friend killed himself.
The impostor gives the young woman his revolver for her protection.
In the morning, the other man discovers that the doctor has vanished and the three conduct a search for him.
The other man separates and goes outside, where he is crushed by a large statue of a bear.
The young woman and the impostor discover the body of the doctor in the snow and conclude that the killer can only be either of them.
The young woman pulls the revolver on the impostor and shoots at him, before returning to the mansion.
She goes upstairs and discovers the judge very much alive, who explains how he persuaded the doctor to help him fake his death.
He adds that he intends to poison himself, leaving the young woman as the last remaining survivor, who must hang herself and fulfil the rhyme, or be punished by the law instead.
As the judge is explaining his plan, having taken a fatal dose of poison, the impostor reappears, alive.
As he dies, the judge realises his plan has failed, and the young woman and the impostor kiss in relief.
They see the cat sitting with the fruit tray, with only two Indians attached.

After spending the night at a doss house, where he has taken pictures for a book of art photographs, the photographer is late for a photo shoot with a model at his studio, which in turn makes him late for a shoot with other models later in the morning.
He grows bored and frustrated with the models and walks off, leaving them and the production staff in the lurch.
As he leaves the studio, two teenage aspiring models ask to speak to him, but he brushes them off and drives off to visit an antique shop near a park.
Wandering into the park, the photographer furtively takes photographs of two lovers, an older man in his 60s and a lady in her 30s.
He follows them in a secluded area in the park.
Then, he leaves, but the woman is furious at being photographed and pursues the photographer, demanding his film and attempting to take his camera.
He refuses, and continues to photograph her as she runs away.
The photographer then meets his agent for lunch and notices a man following him and looking into his car.
The photographer returns to his studio to find the woman, who asks desperately for the film.
They have a conversation and flirt, but he deliberately hands her a different roll of film.
She, in turn, gives him a false telephone number.
The photographer makes several blow-ups of the film of the woman and her lover, which reveal the woman appearing to look worriedly at a person lurking in the trees with a pistol.
The photographer returns to the darkroom to blow up the photograph repeatedly, until the coarsening grain suggests a body lying in the undergrowth.
The photographer excitedly calls his agent, claiming that his impromptu photo session may have saved a man's life.
He is then disturbed by a knock on the door from the teenage girls.
They have a sexual encounter in the studio before he falls asleep.
After awakening, he learns that the girls hope he will photograph them, but is distracted by a detail in one of his blow-ups.
He tells them to leave, saying, "Tomorrow!
The photographer examines a blurred figure on the ground under a bush in the blow-up, which he suspects is the dead body of a man shot by the gunman.
As evening falls, he goes back to the park without his camera and finds the body, but is scared off by the sound of a twig breaking.
He returns to his studio to find it ransacked, with all of the negatives and prints gone except for one very grainy blow-up of what is possibly the body.
After driving into town, he sees the woman and follows her into a club, where a rock band are performing a song.
A buzzing noise in the guitarist's amplifier angers him so much that he smashes his guitar and throws its neck into the crowd.
The crowd, previously disengaged, fights over the guitar neck.
The photographer grabs the neck and runs out of the club, with much of the crowd chasing after him; once he is away from the crowd, he tosses the neck away and walks on.
A passer-by picks up the neck and examines it, but also discards it.
At a drug-drenched party in a house on the river, the photographer asks his cannabis-addled agent to come to the park as a witness, but cannot convince him of what has happened.
Instead, the photographer joins the party at his agent's insistence and wakes up in the house at sunrise.
He then returns to the park alone, only to find that the body is gone.
The photographer watches a mime troupe perform a mock-tennis match at the park, and picks up the imaginary ball and throws it back to the two players when asked.
As he watches the mimes continue to play, the sound of the ball being played is heard.
His image then fades away, leaving only the grass.
